attachment.content:
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- bump-version: Raise the project's version — a minor bump by default. Use when the owner says "bump version".
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- writing-migration-plans: How to order the phases of an implementation or migration plan so nothing stalls mid-run — front-load the out-of-band setup, collapse the review gates into one stacked-PR pass, leave only executable steps — and how to keep its tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use when writing or reviewing a migration plan or a phased implementation plan, and when working through one's tracking issue.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.

input.body:
A sweep of `packs/**/*.md` found the corpus carries four shapes — `RULES.md`, `skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, `tasks/<name>/task.md`, `README.md` — plus files that are none of them, and a `task.md` convention that has drifted from what `agent_model` says.

Owner's rulings on the sweep: `README.md` is a sanctioned shape; a pack without `RULES.md` is fine; a task without `task.md` is fine. What is not fine:

**1. An agentless task carrying a `task.md`.** Six tasks declare `agent_model: 'none'` and still carry one — `claudinite-growth/tasks/usage-fold` and all five `sheepdog/tasks/fleet-*`. Each of those files opens by saying it is not agent instructions ("This task runs no agent … the human-facing record of what that worker does"), so `task.md` there means the opposite of what it means everywhere else. Rename each to `README.md` in place (owner's call — content is real and belongs beside the code it describes), and land the rule as a blocking check so the drift cannot come back.

**2. `claudinite-growth/RULES.md` pointing at the task contract.** A rule whose content is "go read this skill" costs every session in every declaring repo its tokens to say what the skill's own trigger description already says. The pointer belongs in the pack README; the rule goes. The second rule there ("Wanting a job to run in Actions") is a real in-session judgment call and stays.

**3. `packs/static-website/RELEASE.md`.** It is a procedure wanted at authoring time — the release standard a site repo conforms to, reached only by following a link. Same shape as `scheduled-tasks.md` before #975: it should be a skill.

**4. The dangling `doc:` in `task-declaration-shape.mjs`.** Already fixed by #975 — verify and close out.

`packs/chrome-extension-release/RELEASE.md` is the same shape, but the owner's call there is that the whole pack should collapse into `packs/chrome-extension` — its own change, tracked separately.

---

**Done** in #1056: all four. The renames landed with `task-md-only-when-agentic` (blocking) behind them, the `RULES.md` pointer is gone with the pack README carrying it, `static-website/RELEASE.md` is now the `static-site-releases` skill, and `task-declaration-shape`'s `doc:` was confirmed fixed by #975 (nothing in the tree names `scheduled-tasks.md` any more).

The pack collapse is #1057.

---

Owner's call, from the `packs/**/*.md` sweep (#1055): `packs/chrome-extension-release/RELEASE.md` is the same non-conforming shape as `static-website/RELEASE.md`, but the answer here is not "make it a skill" — the whole `chrome-extension-release` pack should collapse into `packs/chrome-extension`.

Its own change, and not a small one — what it has to carry:

- The **declaration**: members declare `chrome-extension-release` in `.claudinite-checks.json`. A pack that stops existing must not leave a member with an undeclarable id, so this needs a migration record that rewrites the declaration (and drops the now-redundant entry where `chrome-extension` is already there).
- The **fingerprint**: `chrome-extension-release` is fingerprinted on the release orchestrator and `chrome-extension` on `manifest.json`. Collapsing merges an opt-in release standard into an always-on coding pack — every extension repo would start carrying the release checks whether or not it ships. Whether the release rules stay relevance-gated on the orchestrator, or the pack keeps two activation tiers, is the design question to settle first.
- The **vendored stubs** (`stubs/workflows/`, `stubs/actions/`) and the `chrome-release-vendoring` migration that materializes them.
- `RELEASE.md` itself, plus the checks whose `doc:` points at it, `bump-version`'s link, and the `.github/workflows/README.md` reference that calls it the standard.
- The two packs' `ruleRoutingGuidance`, which currently define each other by exclusion.

Blocked on nothing; wanted after #1056 lands so the static-website half is settled first.

---

## Design — settled

**Activation is structural, not a second opt-in.** One pack, `chrome-extension`, fingerprinted on `manifest.json` as it is today. The release half stays effectively opt-in by being **relevance-gated on the repo actually shipping the pipeline** — a tracked `.github/workflows/*.yml` named `Release to Chrome Store`, the same fingerprint `chrome-extension-release` used as its `detect`. That is the corpus's own relevance-first doctrine, and it is strictly better than a pack-level opt-in: a repo that ships gets the checks without anyone remembering to declare a second pack, and a repo that only *codes* an extension sees none of them. It also honours "prefer a structural classifier to a hand-set field" — a config key would be the same fact, typed by hand, once per repo.

Six of the seven declared checks are not self-gating today (`cer/release-config` *requires* `.github/release.config`, `cer/release-layout` requires `PRIVACY.md`, `cer/readme-sections` requires README sections, …) — pack-level opt-in was what kept them off a non-shipping repo. Each gains `relevantWhen.someTrackedFileContains` on the orchestrator, which is where that gate belongs.

**The `cer/` check ids do not change.** A member's `accept` entries name rules by id; renaming an id silently orphans an acceptance and the finding returns with no carrier to move it. The prefix outliving the pack it was named for is the cheaper of the two costs, said at the declaration.

**The declaration converges through the rename map.** `RENAMED_PACKS` gains `chrome-extension-release → chrome-extension`, so a member reads correctly the moment the mount lands, whether or not its declaration has been rewritten — the same tolerance the 2026-08-19 pack renames used. A pack-owned migration record at `chrome-extension` version 3 carries `renameDeclaredPacks: true` to converge the declaration itself. Every member with the release pack also has the coding pack (it is its `requires`), so the rewrite collides on **every** member: `applyPackRenames` gains a merge — one surviving entry, with the two entries' `config`/`rules`/`accept` subtrees merged rather than one of them dropped.

No engine version bump: the tolerance ships with the mount, and the record is version-gated on the pack's own number, so no canary release gate is involved.

## Phases

1. **Engine tolerance and the record** — the rename map entry, the merge in `applyPackRenames`, the pack-owned record. Blocks everything member-facing.
2. **The move** — release modules, stubs, task, the vendoring migration record and `RELEASE.md` (→ a `chrome-store-releases` skill, since a `RELEASE.md` at the new home would be the same non-conforming shape #1055 just cleared) into `packs/chrome-extension/`, with the relevance gates added as they land.
3. **The sweep** — delete the old directory, repoint every inbound reference (canon `.claudinite-checks.json` barrier exceptions, `.github/workflows/README.md`, `packs/README.md`, `bump-version`, the sibling packs' prose), re-render `directory.GENERATED.md`.
4. **Proof** — the moved tests, a rehearsal fixture for the shape this change newly exposes (an extension repo that codes but does not ship, which must stay green), full suite, `check_the_world`, `check_the_work`.

---

content.content:
# chrome-extension-release pack

The release & Chrome-Web-Store publication standard for our extensions — the reusable workflows' contract, the setup steps, the manual store actions (`RELEASE.md`), the **vendored release set** (`stubs/workflows/` + `stubs/actions/`, materialized into each consumer's own `.github/`), and the conformance checks. **Opt-in**: a project declares it in `.claudinite-checks.json` when it's ready to ship (a `manifest.json` alone does not pull it in). Declaring it is the cue to vendor the release machinery — the migration apply pass materializes the set (the `chrome-release-vendoring` migration), the pack's checks keep it in shape, and setup opens the one-time first-publication issue. GitHub only resolves a reusable workflow / composite action from a repo's own `.github/`, so the pack holds the templates and each consumer hosts a managed copy — no cross-repo `@main` dependency.

Fingerprint: a repo already carrying the standard's `Release to Chrome Store` orchestrator (a workflow with that name — or a legacy pre-rename name like `Release` — that wires the create-package reusable, whether via the vendored local `./.github/workflows/chrome-extension-create-package.yml` or the pre-vendoring canon call `@main`). `--init` uses it to seed the pack into a fresh declaration (including a repo that shipped release before this pack existed); the marker only *suspects* the pack, so it never forces or forbids the declaration afterward.

## Checks

The release set's conformance rules. Every one of them is about a release that would otherwise fail — or publish the wrong thing — only once it reached the store.

| Check | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| `cer/release-workflows` | high | correctness | check: blocking |
| `cer/template-tokens` | high | correctness | check: blocking |
| `cer/release-config` | high | correctness | check: blocking |
| `cer/version-sync` | high | correctness | check: blocking |
| `cer/release-layout` | medium | correctness | check: blocking |
| `cer/readme-sections` | low | complexity | check: blocking |
| `cer/privacy-permission-alignment` | critical | legal | check: blocking |
| `cer/permission-added-store-issue` | high | legal | check: advisory |
=== chrome-extension README ===
# chrome-extension pack

Active when a `manifest.json` declares `manifest_version` — the MV3 build/runtime gotchas that apply while you're *coding* an extension. Mostly prose (`RULES.md`); the gotchas with a static signature in the source are checks.

Releasing and Chrome-Web-Store publication are a separate, opt-in concern: the [`chrome-extension-release`](../chrome-extension-release/README.md) pack (its `RELEASE.md` standard + conformance checks), declared when the project is ready to ship.

## What the pack carries

The gotchas themselves live in [`RULES.md`](RULES.md), grouped by the surface each concerns —
service worker, content scripts, permissions and host access, sign-in and tokens, extension UI
surfaces, and introspecting a service worker over CDP. The index below is held against that prose by
`packs-tests/rule-index.test.mjs`, which is what makes a second listing safe here: an earlier
hand-kept one drifted into claiming a prose rule that never existed (#777).

## Rules (`RULES.md`)

| Rule | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| Passing a path from a service worker | high | correctness | prose: 68 words |
| Wanting import/export in extension code | medium | correctness | prose: 51 words |
| Assembling a shared global across files | high | correctness | prose: 51 words |
| Accumulating state in a re-injected file | high | correctness | prose: 22 words |
| Loading module code into a content script | high | correctness | prose: 118 words + check (`content-script-module-syntax`) |
| Adding an import to a content-script module | high | correctness | prose: 30 words |
| Keeping that webaccessibleresources list correct | high | correctness | prose: 29 words |
| Matching a host with chrome.events.UrlFilter | high | correctness | prose: 63 words |
| Running on third-party pages without a warning | high | legal | prose: 60 words |
| Starting the worker on a granted permission | medium | correctness | prose: 43 words |
| A listed host's fetch failing in-browser | medium | correctness | prose: 42 words |
| Reaching your own backend | medium | correctness | prose: 35 words |
| Authenticating an extension to a JWT-validating backend | critical | correctness | prose: 83 words |
| Refreshing a token silently | medium | correctness | prose: 28 words |
| Refreshing silently with two accounts | medium | correctness | prose: 41 words |
| Storing a token | critical | correctness | prose: 38 words |
| Keeping a token across a restart | medium | correctness | prose: 30 words |
| Knowing whether your side panel is open | low | correctness | prose: 37 words |
| Opening the side panel programmatically | medium | correctness | prose: 15 words |
| Putting a menu on the toolbar icon | low | correctness | prose: 30 words |
| Recreating menu items on startup | medium | correctness | prose: 30 words |
| Awaiting a chrome. callback API inside Runtime.evaluate | low | correctness | prose: 34 words |
| Reading a worker value over CDP | low | correctness | prose: 30 words |
| Attaching to a dormant worker | low | correctness | prose: 39 words |

## Checks

| Check | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| `content-script-module-syntax` | high | correctness | check: blocking |
| `declarative-content-set-icon` | medium | correctness | check: blocking |

# chrome-extension pack

Active when a `manifest.json` declares `manifest_version` — the MV3 build/runtime gotchas that apply while you're *coding* an extension. Mostly prose (`RULES.md`); the gotchas with a static signature in the source are checks.

Releasing and Chrome-Web-Store publication are a separate, opt-in concern: the [`chrome-extension-release`](../chrome-extension-release/README.md) pack (its `RELEASE.md` standard + conformance checks), declared when the project is ready to ship.

## What the pack carries

The gotchas themselves live in [`RULES.md`](RULES.md), grouped by the surface each concerns —
service worker, content scripts, permissions and host access, sign-in and tokens, extension UI
surfaces, and introspecting a service worker over CDP. The index below is held against that prose by
`packs-tests/rule-index.test.mjs`, which is what makes a second listing safe here: an earlier
hand-kept one drifted into claiming a prose rule that never existed (#777).

## Rules (`RULES.md`)

| Rule | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| Passing a path from a service worker | high | correctness | prose: 68 words |
| Wanting import/export in extension code | medium | correctness | prose: 51 words |
| Assembling a shared global across files | high | correctness | prose: 51 words |
| Accumulating state in a re-injected file | high | correctness | prose: 22 words |
| Loading module code into a content script | high | correctness | prose: 118 words + check (`content-script-module-syntax`) |
| Adding an import to a content-script module | high | correctness | prose: 30 words |
| Keeping that webaccessibleresources list correct | high | correctness | prose: 29 words |
| Matching a host with chrome.events.UrlFilter | high | correctness | prose: 63 words |
| Running on third-party pages without a warning | high | legal | prose: 60 words |
| Starting the worker on a granted permission | medium | correctness | prose: 43 words |
| A listed host's fetch failing in-browser | medium | correctness | prose: 42 words |
| Reaching your own backend | medium | correctness | prose: 35 words |
| Authenticating an extension to a JWT-validating backend | critical | correctness | prose: 83 words |
| Refreshing a token silently | medium | correctness | prose: 28 words |
| Refreshing silently with two accounts | medium | correctness | prose: 41 words |
| Storing a token | critical | correctness | prose: 38 words |
| Keeping a token across a restart | medium | correctness | prose: 30 words |
| Knowing whether your side panel is open | low | correctness | prose: 37 words |
| Opening the side panel programmatically | medium | correctness | prose: 15 words |
| Putting a menu on the toolbar icon | low | correctness | prose: 30 words |
| Recreating menu items on startup | medium | correctness | prose: 30 words |
| Awaiting a chrome. callback API inside Runtime.evaluate | low | correctness | prose: 34 words |
| Reading a worker value over CDP | low | correctness | prose: 30 words |
| Attaching to a dormant worker | low | correctness | prose: 39 words |

## Checks

| Check | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| `content-script-module-syntax` | high | correctness | check: blocking |
| `declarative-content-set-icon` | medium | correctness | check: blocking |

## Skills

[**chrome-store-releases**](skills/chrome-store-releases/SKILL.md) is the release standard itself — the vendored workflows and composite actions, `.github/release.config`, versioning and the packaged artifact, the store secrets, the README install sections, and the manual Chrome Web Store steps. It is the contract the `cer/` checks judge against, reached when a pipeline is being set up or debugged rather than carried by every session in the repo.

## Task

`tasks/store-release/` fires the repo's daily release: agentless, `code_work` only, dispatching the vendored daily workflow. It absorbed that workflow's own 00:30 cron so the Claudinite scheduler stays the repo's only one, and its precondition declines on a repo that does not publish.""", 1)

input.body:
Closes #1057. Three commits: the engine tolerance, the collapse, the sweep.

## The design question the issue named

Merging an opt-in release standard into an always-on coding pack looks like it turns the release checks on for every extension repo. It does not, because **the release half's activation was always structural** — `chrome-extension-release`'s `detect` was the orchestrator workflow's name, and declaring the pack was a second copy of that same fact which each repo had to remember to write.

So the fact is now read where it is used: `shipsReleasePipeline` gates the coded rule, all seven `cer/` declared checks carry the same test as their `relevantWhen`, and `store-release`'s precondition asks it of the `release` signal. A repo that only *codes* an extension is asked for no release config, no privacy page and no README release sections. A repo that publishes gets all of it without declaring anything.

**Two signals, either one enough** — the orchestrator's `name:`, or a `.github/release.config`. Each alone leaves the rule that judges it unreachable: gate only on the name and a repo that renamed its orchestrator loses every release check *including the one that tells it to rename it back*; gate only on the config and `cer/release-config`, whose whole job is a missing config, can never fire. The orchestrator is matched by name and never by path, because the canon hosts files at those paths and would otherwise fingerprint itself.

The gate is spelled three times — the coded rule, the JSON (which cannot import), and the scheduler signal (the engine may not import a pack) — so a test runs all three over one matrix of repo shapes and fails if any copy drifts. Seen failing on each copy in turn.

## Members

`RENAMED_PACKS` gains `chrome-extension-release → chrome-extension`, so a member activates the right pack the moment the mount lands, declaration converged or not; a pack-owned record at `chrome-extension` version 3 converges the declaration itself. No engine version bump, so no canary release gate is involved.

The rename **collides on every member**, because the absorbed pack's `requires` meant everyone declaring it declared the survivor too. `applyPackRenames` now merges instead of producing a duplicate: first occurrence keeps its position, its own values win a conflict, arrays union, and an object absorbed into a plain-string entry promotes it. # Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, name the folders the change touched** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Leave out test folders, README edits, and above all any file whose diff is comments only.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

committed default pinned to dev, prod config injected only by the release pipeline, and — the part
provenance alone can't give — **App Check attestation** so only store-installed builds reach the
prod backend. Declared when a project approaches shipping, like
[chrome-extension](../chrome-extension/README.md).

> **Status: standard decided ahead of first exercise.** Distilled from missingbulb/TLDR's worked
> AWS split (account/stack/config/CI layers, its provenance-only gap explicitly noted) and decided
> for Firebase in missingbulb/ShoutsAndWhispers `docs/ENVIRONMENTS.md`; no project has run a
> release through it yet. Expect refinement — and conformance checks, mirroring
> chrome-extension's release half — when the first release exercises it.

# barriers pack

Enforce a **directed folder-access graph** in a repo: declare that the files under one set of folders may not reference another, and the check finds every crossing reference — across all languages and file types. The mechanism other packs compose their separation rules on.

Declared like any pack (no fingerprint — wanting structural segregation is the project's own call; a pack that needs it names `barriers` in its `requires`). Check-only, no prose: the finding is the instruction.

## Declaring barriers

A repo states its graph as `config.rules` on its **barriers pack entry** in `.claudinite-checks.json` — an array of rules. A rule is the unit; each rule owns its exceptions.

Adopting the pack without a graph is a silent no-op, so adoption asks one question — what the barriers are *for* ([the adoption interview](../README.md#adoption-interview-questions)): the owner's answer is recorded verbatim as `answers.goals` on the entry, and the edge list below is distilled from it.

```json
{
  "packs": [
    "basics",
    {
      "id": "barriers",
      "config": {
        "rules": [
          { "from": "src", "to": "tests", "reason": "source must not know about its tests" },
          { "between": ["client", "server"], "allow": ["shared", "contracts"],
            "reason": "client and server integrate only through the shared contract" },
          { "from": "dev/requirements", "to": "*", "allow": ["README.md"],
            "reason": "requirements is a pure sink — it references nothing outside itself" },
          { "from": ["engine", "cli", "loader.js"], "to": "plugins/*", "matchNames": true,
            "reason": "the host must not know the specific plugins it loads",
            "except": [
              { "path": "engine/registry.js", "to": ["plugins/legacy"],
                "reason": "temporary bridge during the plugin split — tracked in #123" }
            ] }
        ]
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

Rule fields:

- **`from`** — the folder(s) guarded: a folder, a file, `"."` for the whole repo, or an **array** of them. Naming the core folders positively (`["engine", "cli", "loader.js"]`) keeps content, catalogs, and config naturally out of scope — no carve-outs needed for them. A `from` entry may be a single engine file living *inside* a content tree (`loader.js` next to the plugins it loads); that file is guarded without the tree around it being scanned.
- **`to`** — what must not be referenced: a folder, `"<folder>/*"` (a glob barring **every direct child directory**, enumerated from the tree — files directly under `<folder>` stay reachable), `"*"` (isolation/sink: `from` may reference nothing outside itself), or an **array** of the folder/glob forms. An empty glob expansion is a blocking `config` finding, never a silent no-op: a renamed folder must not disarm the barrier.
- **`{ between: [a, b] }`** — sugar for a mutual ban (both `a → b` and `b → a`).
- **`{ siblings: "<folder>", to, ... }`** — guard **each direct child directory** of `<folder>` in
  turn (instead of `from`; the children are enumerated from the tree at scan time, and an empty
  expansion is a blocking `config` finding). `to: "<folder>/*"` gives **mutual sibling
  separation** — every child may reference its own files but no sibling's; `to: "*"` gives
  **per-child isolation**, each child confined to itself plus the `allow` list. The form for
  "these subfolders are independent units" without enumerating (and maintaining) one edge per
  unit.
- **`scope: "imports"`** — restrict the edge to **relative import/require specifiers in code
  files** (`import x from '…'`, `import('…')`, `require('…')` in `.js`/`.mjs`/`.ts`-family
  sources, matched across line breaks), resolved as **module edges**: file-relative only with
  extension/index completion, no bare or root-relative strings, no name/unique-filename layers,
  and an index-less directory import is breakage rather than a crossing. Prose, docs, and
  comments stay free to mention — or quote paths into — the barred folders; the coupling class
  this scope polices is the one that crashes at runtime. Default is every resolvable reference;
  incompatible with `matchNames` (a text layer an imports-only edge excludes by definition).
- **`allow: [...]`** (or a single `"allow": "shared"`) — folders reachable despite the ban (a `shared`/`contracts` folder both sides may use). Always implicitly allowed: references *within* the guarded region itself.
- **`matchNames: true`** — opt into the **bare-name layer**: the barred folders' own names are matched as bare words too (see below). `alsoMatchNames: [...]` force-includes non-distinctive names.
- **`matchUniqueFilenames: false`** — opt *out* of the unique-basename layer (on by default). A bare `filename.ext` then resolves only through the path attempts, so a **convention marker** (a filename many folders are meant to carry but only one does yet — `checks.mjs`, `RELEASE.md`) no longer reads as a coupling to that lone folder. Path references and distinctive names still fire.
- **`except: [...]`** — the rule's own exceptions (see [Exceptions](#exceptions-carve-outs-and-reviewed-crossings)).
- **`reason`** — surfaced as the finding's *why*.

Paths are repo-relative prefixes; both `/` and `\` separators are accepted. A malformed rule — overlapping `from`/`to`, an empty prefix, an unknown property — is a blocking `config` finding, not a silent no-op.

### The whole-repo form

`from: "."` guards the entire repo, carved down by `except` carve-out strings. It is the safe-by-default posture (a new top-level file is guarded until excepted), at the cost of listing the content trees to subtract:

questions.question: The 51 crossings split into two kinds. Which are "such references"?

options.label: Both — a pack references no sibling, ever (Recommended)
options.description: All 51 go. A pack becomes a closed unit: it may name a sibling in routing metadata but never link into one. Pointers to a canonical skill get replaced by naming it in words ("the git-github-advanced skill") with no path — findable by an agent, not a coupling.

options.label: Only the discussion, keep the procedure pointers

Keep the ~39 links to a named canonical skill (basics/RULES.md → git-github-advanced, sheepdog task docs → writing-tasks), since basics' own rule says point at B rather than re-spell it.

options.label: Both, and duplicate what was pointed at
options.description: Purge all 51 and copy the pointed-at guidance into each pack that needed it, so nothing is lost. Costs duplication that basics/RULES.md currently forbids, and the copies drift.

questions.question: Every pack.mjs carries `ruleRoutingGuidance.excludes`, which names the neighbouring pack by bare word ("store submission — that is chrome-extension"). packs/README.md mandates it: "name the pack that owns the other side". Does it stay?

options.label: Stays — it is routing data, not discussion (Recommended)
options.description: A bare name in a structured field is how a lesson gets routed to the right pack; the barrier's default settings do not fire on bare names anyway. Same for `requires`. No change to packs/README.md.

options.label: Goes too — no pack names another anywhere
options.description: Purge the excludes column and rewrite the convention in packs/README.md. The routing table then says only what a pack is not about, without saying who owns it — a lesson lands by search rather than by pointer.

questions.question: How strict should the barrier rule be about exceptions?

options.label: Zero exceptions (Recommended)
options.description: The rule takes no `except` entries. Anything that seems to need one is a signal the content is in the wrong pack — which is what the sweep should fix rather than excuse.

options.label: Reviewed exceptions where a pack's job IS another pack
options.description: sheepdog and claudinite-dashboard exist to operate on what other packs produce, so a handful of reviewed `except` entries with reasons. Honest about the real dependency, at the cost of a list that tends to grow.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, name the folders the change touched** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Leave out test folders, README edits, and above all any file whose diff is comments only.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- bump-version: Raise the project's version — a minor bump by default. Use when the owner says "bump version".
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-branch-status: Assess one branch's landed status — merged, already-in-main, superseded, orphaned, or genuine unmerged work — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single branch is safe to delete, judging by content not the ref's name (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-branches task hands you branches to assess).
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- writing-claudinite-skills: Authoring or changing a skill in the Claudinite corpus — SKILL.md conventions, where a skill's checks and tests live, catalog and pack wiring. Use when creating or editing a pack's skills/<name>/ in the canon; a consumer project's own agent docs are authoring-agent-docs' turf.
- writing-migration-plans: How to order the phases of an implementation or migration plan so nothing stalls mid-run — front-load the out-of-band setup, collapse the review gates into one stacked-PR pass, leave only executable steps — and how to keep its tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use when writing or reviewing a migration plan or a phased implementation plan, and when working through one's tracking issue.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.mjs or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including Markdown ones — format is part of the design pass, never a speed shortcut.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, handing the viewer a file to save, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.

Claudinite loaded, 9 packs, 45 checks, 13,000 rule tokens, 22 available skills, 530 personal preference tokens.

I probed the tree with a `barriers` rule (`siblings: "packs"` → `packs/*`) — the pack already has exactly this capability, so no new code is needed to enforce it. It finds **51 crossings across 22 packs**, and they fall into three different shapes. Three questions before I purge:

questions.question: The 51 crossings split into two kinds. One is what you flagged — prose in pack A discussing pack B (firebase-release's "like chrome-extension", jwt's "obtaining the token in a browser — chrome-extension"). The other is a pointer to a canonical procedure in another pack: basics/RULES.md → git-github's merge skill, sheepdog's task docs → claudinite-growth's writing-tasks skill, headless-browser/RULES.md → basics' writing-tests skill. Which do I purge?

options.label: Both — a pack references nothing outside itself (Recommended)
options.description: All 51 go, and the barrier stays on to keep them gone. Where A currently points at B's procedure, A states what it needs in one line and stops — the skill's own trigger description is what makes B findable, not a link from A. Strictest, and the only version a check can hold.

options.label: Only the discussion; keep procedure pointers
options.description: Purge prose that talks about a sibling pack (~20 crossings), keep a link when A delegates a procedure to B (~30). Needs an `allow`/`except` list of skill paths in the barrier config, maintained as skills move.

options.label: Only the discussion, and no barrier
options.description: One-off cleanup of the prose you flagged, no standing check. Cheapest now; the class comes straight back — it is how all 51 got there.

options.label: Keep — it is routing data, not discussion (Recommended)
options.description: A bare pack name in a structured field, not prose about another pack. The barrier leaves it alone by default (bare names only match with `matchNames: true`), so nothing extra is needed.

options.label: Purge those too
options.description: excludes stops naming packs and describes the excluded territory instead ("store submission and release cadence"). The directory table stops routing by name, and packs/README.md's convention gets rewritten in the same change.

options.description: Rewrite the stub comments (they are current files describing a live pipeline) and re-materialize; leave the two migration records, which describe arrangements true when they were written — the repo's rule against editing historical records.

options.label: Leave both
options.description: Neither is a pack referencing a sibling pack — the stubs are templates for a consumer's .github/, and the name only appears in comments. Smallest diff.

options.label: Change both
options.description: Purge the name everywhere it appears, records included, so a grep for the retired pack returns nothing at all.

input.title: Collapse chrome-extension-release into chrome-extension, and stop packs discussing each other
input.body:
Closes #1057. Four commits: the engine tolerance, the collapse, the reference sweep, and the cross-pack prose purge.

## The design question the issue named

Merging an opt-in release standard into an always-on coding pack looks like it turns the release checks on for every extension repo. It does not, because **the release half's activation was always structural** — `chrome-extension-release`'s `detect` was the orchestrator workflow's name, and declaring the pack was a second copy of that same fact which each repo had to remember to write.

So the fact is now read where it is used: `shipsReleasePipeline` gates the coded rule, all seven `cer/` declared checks carry the same test as their `relevantWhen`, and `store-release`'s precondition asks it of the `release` signal. A repo that only *codes* an extension is asked for no release config, no privacy page and no README release sections. A repo that publishes gets all of it without declaring anything.

**Two signals, either one enough** — the orchestrator's `name:`, or a `.github/release.config`. Each alone leaves the rule that judges it unreachable: gate only on the name and a repo that renamed its orchestrator loses every release check *including the one that tells it to rename it back*; gate only on the config and `cer/release-config`, whose whole job is a missing config, can never fire. The orchestrator is matched by name and never by path, because the canon hosts files at those paths and would otherwise fingerprint itself.

The gate is spelled three times — the coded rule, the JSON (which cannot import), and the scheduler signal (the engine may not import a pack) — so a test runs all three over one matrix of repo shapes and fails if any copy drifts. Seen failing on each copy in turn.

## Members

`RENAMED_PACKS` gains `chrome-extension-release → chrome-extension`, so a member activates the right pack the moment the mount lands, declaration converged or not; a pack-owned record at `chrome-extension` version 3 converges the declaration itself. No engine version bump, so no canary release gate is involved.

The rename **collides on every member**, because the absorbed pack's `requires` meant everyone declaring it declared the survivor too. `applyPackRenames` now merges instead of producing a duplicate: first occurrence keeps its position, its own values win a conflict, arrays union, and an object absorbed into a plain-string entry promotes it. Dropping either side would drop the member's own `config`, `rules` and `accept` — acceptances especially, since a dropped one brings its finding straight back.

**The `cer/` ids do not change**, for the same reason: `accept` entries name rules by id.

## A pack does not discuss its neighbours

Reviewing the collapse turned up the wider class: `firebase-release`'s README opened by saying it is declared "like chrome-extension". A `barriers` probe (`siblings: "packs"` → `packs/*`) found **51 such crossings across 22 packs**, in two shapes:

- **Boundary/turf prose** — "sits under X", "that is Y's turf", a whole `## Boundary` section listing what the neighbours own. Purged. It is a second copy of what `ruleRoutingGuidance.excludes` already carries in one machine-read field — the field the pack directory routes a lesson by — so each site now states what the pack does *not* cover without naming who does.
- **Procedure pointers** — a rule delegating a how-to to another pack's skill, a check's `doc:` field, an executable command, and the comments on the dashboard's deliberate duplicates of sheepdog's helpers. Kept: the link is what makes the procedure findable, and restating it in both places is exactly what the corpus forbids.

22 references survive, all in the second class. No standing barrier rule was added — the probe was a measuring instrument, and it is not in the diff.

## Consumer safety

The shape the collapse newly exposes is an extension repo that codes but does not publish — the canon publishes no extension, so its own CI says nothing about it. `packs-tests/rehearsal/fixtures.mjs` gains that shape (`codes-an-extension`), and a pack test asserts every release rule is inert on it.

## Folders touched

- **`engine/pack_loader/`, `engine/migrations/`** — the rename-map entry and the merge in `applyPackRenames`.
- **`engine/scheduler/signals/`** — the `release` signal carries whether the repo publishes, read off the checkout beside the manifest version it already read.
- **`packs/chrome-extension/`** — absorbs the release module, the seven declared checks (each gated), the stubs, the `store-release` task, both migration records, and `RELEASE.md` as the **`chrome-store-releases`** skill; manifest, README and RULES rewritten for one pack.
- **`packs/firebase`, `firebase-release`, `google-identity`, `jwt`, `web-speech`, `headless-browser`, `executable-requirements`, `spec-driven-product`, `web-scraping`, `git-github`, `sheepdog`, `claudinite-growth`, `claudinite-lifecycle`, `basics`** — neighbour prose removed, and in the release packs' case references to the pack that no longer exists.
- **`.github/`** — the core workflows README, and the retired pre-vendoring release copies' own naming.
- **`packs-tests/rehearsal/`** — the fixture shape above.
- Versions bumped on every pack whose content changed; `packs/directory.GENERATED.md` re-rendered by its test.

The two migration records keep their wording — they describe arrangements true when they were written.

## Verification

- `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` — 2200 pass, 0 fail.
- `check_the_work --changed --base origin/main` — exit 0.
- `check_the_world` — 0 blocking, 61 advisory (all pre-existing).
- The merge and both drift-guard directions seen red before the code that fixes them; the crossing count re-measured after the purge.

Purged, on [#1060](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1060) (same branch — it corrects a line that PR touched).

**What I found by probing rather than grepping:** the `barriers` pack already has the exact capability (`siblings: "packs"` → `packs/*`), so I ran it as a measuring instrument — **51 crossings across 22 packs**, not one. Your `firebase-release` line was the visible edge of it.

Per your answers:

- **Boundary/turf prose purged** — [firebase-release](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/claude/non-conforming-markdown-files-1rg113/packs/firebase-release/README.md) ("declared … like chrome-extension", "mirroring chrome-extension's release half"), [jwt](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/claude/non-conforming-markdown-files-1rg113/packs/jwt/README.md) and [google-identity](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/claude/non-conforming-markdown-files-1rg113/packs/google-identity/README.md) handing their edges to named neighbours, [headless-browser](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/claude/non-conforming-markdown-files-1rg113/packs/headless-browser/RULES.md)'s entire `## Boundary` section, [claudinite-lifecycle](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/claude/non-conforming-markdown-files-1rg113/packs/claudinite-lifecycle/README.md) explaining why the task contract lives elsewhere, plus firebase, web-speech, executable-requirements, spec-driven-product, web-scraping, git-github, sheepdog, claudinite-growth. Each now says what it does *not* cover without naming who does — which is what `excludes` already carries, once, in a field the directory reads.
- **Procedure pointers kept** — 22 survive, all of them a rule delegating a *how* to another pack's skill, a check's `doc:`, an executable command, or the dashboard's duplication-guard comments (which must name what they duplicate).
- **`excludes` untouched**; **stubs rewritten**, **migration records left**.
- **No barrier rule in the diff** — the probe was an instrument, removed.

One judgment call I made without asking: `git-github-advanced`'s citation "*per the basics pack's RULES.md*" went too. It supports a rule already stated in full on that line, so it was discussion, not a pointer.

Verification: 2200 tests pass, `check_the_work` exit 0, `check_the_world` 0 blocking / 61 advisory (all pre-existing). Eleven more packs needed version bumps, which the work check caught.
